title: Our response to the TanStack npm supply chain attack
teaser: Mandatory update for macOS users: OpenAI is rotating app signing certificates following a supply chain attack, requiring updates by June 12, 2026.
summary: Following a security incident involving the TanStack npm open-source library, OpenAI confirmed that while two internal employee devices were impacted, there is no evidence that user data or intellectual property was compromised. As a precaution, OpenAI is rotating code-signing certificates for its products across iOS, macOS, and Windows. Users must update their macOS applications by June 12, 2026, to ensure they run versions signed with the new certificates. No action is needed for Windows or iOS apps. This incident prompted the company to accelerate security hardening measures, such as implementing controls like minimumReleaseAge, to defend against future supply chain attacks.
content: We recently identified a security issue involving a common open-source library, TanStack npm, that is part of a broader attack known as Mini Shai-Hulud ⁠ (opens in a new window) . We found no evidence that OpenAI user data was accessed, that our production systems or intellectual property were compromised, or that our software was altered. We have taken decisive steps to protect our user data, systems, and intellectual property. As part of our response, we are taking steps to protect the process that certifies our macOS applications are legitimate OpenAI apps. Update your macOS applications by June 12, 2026 We are updating our security certificates, which will require all macOS users to update their OpenAI apps to the latest versions. This helps prevent any risk, however unlikely, of someone attempting to distribute a fake app that appears to be from OpenAI. You can update safely through an in-app update or at the official links below: The security and privacy of your information are a top priority. We're committed to being transparent and taking quick action when issues arise. We're sharing more technical details and FAQs below. Two employee devices in our corporate environment were impacted by this attack. Upon identification of the malicious activity, we worked quickly to investigate, contain, and take steps to protect our systems. As part of our investigation and response, we engaged a third-party digital forensics and incident response firm. We observed activity consistent with the malware's publicly described behavior, including unauthorized access and credential-focused exfiltration activity, in a limited subset of internal source code repositories to which the two impacted employees had access. We confirmed that only limited credential material was successfully exfiltrated from these code repositories and that no other information or code was impacted. We acted immediately to contain the activity. We isolated impacted systems and identities, revoked user sessions, rotated all credentials across impacted repositories, temporarily restricted code-deployment workflows, and thoroughly scrutinized user and credential behavior. As part of our investigation, we have not observed evidence of impact to customer data, or our intellectual property, and our analysis has not identified misuse of impacted credentials or follow-on access by the threat actor. The impacted source code repositories included signing certificates for our products, including iOS, macOS, and Windows. As a result, we are rotating code-signing certificates as a precaution, which will require macOS users to update their applications. Users do not need to take any action for Windows and iOS apps. Additional guidance will be provided to macOS users regarding these required updates. In addition to rotating certificates, we are coordinating with platform providers to prevent any unauthorized use of these certificates by stopping new notarizations. We have also reviewed all notarization of software using our previous certificates to confirm no unexpected software signing has occurred with these keys, and validated that our published software did not have unauthorized modifications. We have found no evidence of compromise or risk to existing software installations. Once we fully revoke our certificate on June 12, 2026, new downloads and launches of apps signed with the previous certificate will be blocked by macOS security protections. After the Axios incident , we accelerated the deployment of specific security controls and technologies to reduce the impact of supply chain attacks such as this one. Our security response included further hardening of sensitive credential materials used in our CI/CD pipeline, deployment of package manager configurations with controls like minimumReleaseAge, and additional security software to validate the provenance of new packages. This incident occurred during our phased deployment and rollout of these controls, and the two impacted employee devices did not have the updated configurations that would have prevented the download of the newly observed package containing malware. This incident reflects a broader shift in the threat landscape: attackers are increasingly targeting shared software dependencies and development tooling rather than any single company. Modern software is built on a deeply interconnected ecosystem of open-source libraries, package managers, and continuous integration and continuous deployment infrastructure, which means that a vulnerability introduced upstream can propagate widely and quickly across organizations. We are continuing to invest in controls that validate the integrity and provenance of third-party components and to strengthen our defenses against these kinds of ecosystem-level supply chain attacks. Were OpenAI products or user data compromised? No. We have found no evidence that OpenAI products or user data were compromised or exposed. Have you seen malware signed as OpenAI? No. We have found no evidence of malicious software being signed with any of OpenAI's certificates. Do I need to change my password? No. Customer/user passwords and API keys were not affected. What platforms does this affect? Our signing keys for Windows, macOS, iOS, and Android were impacted. All of our applications are being re-signed and released with new certificates. macOS users will need to take action to update by June 12, 2026 for applications to continue functioning. Why are you asking me to update my Mac apps? Updating ensures you are running versions signed with our latest certificate. This certificate helps customers know that software comes from the legitimate developer, OpenAI. Where do I download the updated macOS apps? Only download OpenAI apps from in-app updates or the official webpages below: Do not install apps from links in emails, messages, ads, or third-party download sites. Be cautious of unexpected "OpenAI," "ChatGPT," or "Codex" installers sent through email, text, chat messages, ads, file-sharing links, or third-party download sites. What happens after June 12, 2026? Effective June 12, 2026, older versions of our macOS desktop apps will no longer receive updates or support, and may not be functional. These versions represent the last releases signed with our outdated certificate: ChatGPT Desktop: 1.2026.125 Codex App: 26.506.31421 Codex CLI: 0.130.0 Atlas: 1.2026.119.1 Why are you not revoking the certificate immediately? We have worked to block any further notarization of macOS apps with the impacted notarization material. This means that any fraudulent app posing as an OpenAI app using the impacted certificate will lack notarization, and therefore will be blocked by default by macOS security protections unless a user explicitly bypasses those protections. Because new notarization with the previous certificate is blocked, and because the revocation may cause macOS to block new downloads and first-time launches of apps signed with the previous certificate, we are giving our users until June 12, 2026 to update to minimize disruption. This window will help minimize user risk and allow impacted clients to update through built-in update mechanisms, ensuring they are appropriately remediated. We are working with our partners to monitor for any indicators of misuse of the signing certificate, and will accelerate the revocation timeline if we identify malicious activity during this window.

title: Kuaishou Weighs Outside Capital for Kling AI Video Unit
teaser: Major Chinese AI players face massive valuation talks, signaling a high-stakes race to build the next generation of generative AI tools.
summary: High-profile AI development in China is driving massive corporate restructuring and valuation speculation. Kuaishou placed its AI video unit, Kling, under a board review that may attract outside capital, with rumors placing its valuation near US$20 billion, targeting a US$500 million annualized revenue run rate. Concurrently, former Alibaba Qwen researcher Junyang Lin is reportedly considering raising hundreds of millions for a new AI lab at a US$2 billion valuation. These moves highlight the intense race to commercialize generative AI, especially given competition from giants like ByteDance. The talks show that achieving a high valuation requires not just technology but also converting user interest into durable creator workflows and sufficient margins to sustain compute-intensive operations.
author: Markus Kasanmascheff
content: TL;DR Board Review: Kuaishou has confirmed a board review of Kling AI that may bring outside capital into the video unit. Valuation Terms: A discussed $2 billion round would value Kling near US$20 billion, but Kuaishou has not confirmed terms. Revenue Scale: Kling is being discussed at a US$500 million annualized revenue run rate, roughly double its pre-Lunar New Year level. Product Stakes: Kling's compute needs, creator workflows, and ByteDance competition make product speed central to the review. A Tuesday filing from Chinese internet company Kuaishou put a restructuring of its Kling AI video business on the record, with the board assessing a review that may bring in outside capital for the unit. Investors reacted quickly: Kuaishou shares were up as much as 10% on Tuesday morning after new plans for Kling circulated. Kling AI is Kuaishou's generative-AI video and creative-tool business. It includes AI models and products for creating or editing video, images, sound, and multimodal content from prompts or reference material. Kling is no longer only the subject of outside speculation. Kuaishou has acknowledged that the business may need a different setup as it grows, even though no final deal, investor list, or spin-out format has been disclosed. For now, the filing gives investors an official review to track rather than another market rumor. The review is tied to a product category built around creator workflows rather than a simple social feed feature. Users expect prompt control, editable outputs, and repeatable results that can fit into marketing, entertainment, or social video projects. Kling's product role helps explain why investors are treating it as a business line with its own growth profile. Kuaishou has only put the review itself on the record. Its board is reviewing Kling, and the review may involve outside capital for the unit. Valuation talk and investor names still sit outside the company's own disclosure. Why the Filing Changes the Story Board review moves the discussion from rumor into governance. Directors are not only deciding whether Kling needs more money. They are deciding whether the video business should keep growing as part of the parent company or gain a more direct route to outside backing. One scenario now in circulation points to Tencent joining a round of about $2 billion at a US$20 billion valuation. A valuation at that level would sit well above Runway's reported valuation and close to Kuaishou's own market capitalization. Kuaishou has not backed those figures in its own disclosure, but the numbers help explain why the filing drew immediate investor attention. Kuaishou now has three broad choices to examine: keep Kling fully internal, bring in outside backers while retaining control, or move the business toward a more separate vehicle. Each route would affect management authority, transaction transparency, and how much outsiders can learn about Kling's own economics. Valuation and Revenue Signals Tuesday's stock reaction was not only a headline move. Investors were responding to a possible way to value Kling more directly, not only to a broad statement that Kuaishou is interested in AI. Public shareholders can price optionality around a fast-growing AI product before binding terms arrive, giving Kuaishou an immediate market test before any term sheet is disclosed. Kling's own revenue discussion adds another data point. Current discussion around the unit includes a US$500 million annualized revenue run rate , roughly double the level before Lunar New Year. Annualized run rate is not audited full-year revenue; it projects the current pace over a year. Even with that caveat, the figure places Kling well beyond a small internal experiment and helps explain why shareholders may start separating Kuaishou's established short-video operations from Kling's growth profile. A product with that kind of revenue discussion can become a distinct valuation argument inside a much larger consumer internet company, especially if management later gives investors cleaner figures for revenue, costs, and user demand. A high valuation scenario and a visible revenue pace make execution more visible. A young AI unit can command a rich price when investors believe growth will continue, but the gap between run-rate revenue and a multibillion-dollar valuation puts pressure on Kling to convert user interest into recurring creator activity, paid workflows, and enough margin to justify the scale investors are discussing. Board-level review can move a stock before definitive terms exist when investors think the asset may deserve a separate valuation lens. It also gives analysts a reason to compare Kling's potential separately from Kuaishou's mature short-video advertising and live-streaming operations. A fast-growing AI product can carry a different risk profile from the parent company's established platforms. Future disclosures could give investors a benchmark for measuring whether Kling is growing into its rumored price, with revenue pace, user adoption, and product expansion sitting beside the headline number. Analysts will also be watching whether Kling's revenue comes mostly from casual consumer use, creator subscriptions, enterprise media work, or platform partnerships. Those mixes would imply different margins and different growth durability, even if the top-line run rate looks similar. User mix would also affect how Kuaishou explains the unit to shareholders, because a creator-service business is judged differently from an advertising-supported consumer feature. A clearer breakdown would help investors separate durable usage from short-term launch enthusiasm. How Kling AI's Economics Raise the Stakes Kling's resource case centers on computing power and talent as competition in AI video intensifies. Training upgrades require large runs before creators see better clips, while heavy usage adds inference costs every time users generate video. Product growth can also require workflow tools, localization, moderation, support teams, and customer-facing infrastructure at the same time. AI video generation is especially demanding because each clip combines model inference, frame consistency, motion control, and rendering work. A text chatbot can deliver a short answer in seconds, but video tools must preserve visual coherence across many frames. Higher usage can create a different cost curve from ordinary social-video features. For users, those costs show up as everyday product limits: slow queues, failed renders, inconsistent characters, or weak editing controls can matter as much as the raw model behind a clip. If outside backing materializes, Kling would have more room to add compute, push model updates faster, and support the workflow depth needed for repeat creator use. Professional users also need predictable outputs across multiple attempts, not only one impressive demo clip. Competitive Pressure and Earlier Strategy Signals Kuaishou is making that choice while competing with ByteDance in short video. ByteDance's March 26 expansion of Dreamina Seedance 2.0 audio and video generation through CapCut showed how quickly major Chinese platform groups are turning creator-video AI into a product race rather than a feature experiment. ByteDance is also expanding its Seed AI team across multiple regions. CapCut gives ByteDance a distribution channel for creator tools that already sits inside editing workflows, while Seed AI staffing points to model work behind those products. Together, those moves show why a rival video platform cannot treat generative video as a small add-on if it wants creators to build repeat habits around its tools. Distribution, model development, and editing workflow all reinforce one another in this category, because users can discover a feature, test it, and keep editing inside the same product environment. In November 2025, founder and chief executive officer Cheng Yixiao tied Kling to AI-powered film and television creation . Kling is closer to demanding creator and media workflows, where scene composition, editing habits, and repeat use matter as much as novelty. A creator who builds templates, assets, or project habits around one tool is less likely to switch quickly if the service fits a production routine. For Kuaishou, that kind of workflow lock-in can support revenue beyond one-off experimentation because creators may keep paying for a tool that fits their production habits. Film and television use cases also bring Kling into a higher-expectation category than casual social clips: users may need multiple versions of a scene, consistent styles across assets, and export paths that fit existing editing work.

title: Ilya Sutskever Defends His Role in 2023 Altman Ouster
teaser: The OpenAI legal battle centers on whether commercial growth compromised its original nonprofit mission, with multi-billion dollar stakes adding intense pressure.
summary: The ongoing legal dispute over OpenAI's governance revolves around whether its commercial expansion compromised its founding nonprofit mission. Key figures like Ilya Sutskever defended his role in the 2023 Sam Altman ouster, arguing it was a necessary move to protect the organization from failing trust and safety protocols. This is juxtaposed against massive financial stakes, including Greg Brockman's reported $30 billion stake and large secondary sales of $6.6 billion in employee equity. The core conflict is whether the company abandoned its non-profit commitments (warned about in 2017) for-profit growth. The dispute, involving claims of broken board trust, fluctuating leadership, and vast wealth accumulation, is fundamentally a struggle over corporate control and the institution's legal structure.
author: Markus Kasanmascheff
content: TL;DR Trial Testimony: Ilya Sutskever is defending his role in Sam Altman's November 2023 ouster through recent trial testimony. Board Argument: Sutskever said he acted to protect OpenAI and framed the vote as a response to broken trust. Mission Fight: The case is testing whether OpenAI's commercial growth overwhelmed the nonprofit mission its founders described in 2017. Safety Fallout: Sutskever left OpenAI in May 2024, launched Safe Superintelligence, and kept the governance dispute alive. Ilya Sutskever, former OpenAI chief scientist, is defending his role in Sam Altman's November 2023 ouster through recent trial testimony. His account puts that board crisis back at the center of Elon Musk's lawsuit over OpenAI's direction. In his testimony, Sutskever said he acted because he "didn't want it [OpenAI] to be destroyed." He is presenting that explanation as a mission defense. His argument is that the board vote was meant to protect OpenAI rather than to settle a personal feud with Altman. Altman's removal was, according to Sutskever's testimony , a Hail Mary to save OpenAI, backed by more than 50 pages of allegations that Altman repeatedly misled the board and executives. The allegations remain testimony, not a court finding. His account still gives the defense a clearer mechanism: in his telling, the vote followed a long collapse of trust, not a sudden personality clash. Sutskever's safety claim adds another board-duty layer. OpenAI was, in his account, not conducive to safety, which narrows the dispute from whether Altman won an internal political fight to whether directors believed the company could still manage AI risk under his leadership. The claim remains contested testimony, but it explains why Sutskever keeps tying the vote to mission rather than control. Sutskever's testimony also carries unusually large personal stakes. His stake was worth about $7 billion, while Greg Brockman separately recently put his holding at around $30 billion worth of OpenAI shares . The financial stakes help explain why the trial keeps circling back to motive. Control of OpenAI now carries extraordinary personal wealth as well as ideological stakes. Any board decision can affect the lab's mission, product direction, and the fortunes of leaders whose holdings grew with the company's commercial rise. Money alone does not explain the dispute, but it changes its scale. A governance fight inside OpenAI now reaches a company tied to leading AI products, large cloud commitments, and the reputations of executives whose financial upside grew with the lab's commercial transformation. For a court weighing motive, those incentives make each governance claim harder to separate from wealth, control, and strategic leverage. How the 2023 OpenAI Crisis Returned to Court November 2023 remains the key historical reference point for the testimony. During the 2023 board revolt , Altman was temporarily removed before returning after the board lost support. More than 700 employees then threatened to quit, turning a governance vote into a company-wide emergency. Employee resistance showed how little separation remained between board authority and company operations. Directors could cast a formal vote, but they still needed engineers, researchers, and senior managers to keep model development moving. Once workers signaled that they would follow Altman rather than the board, governance authority and operational control no longer pointed in the same direction. Microsoft was preparing for a rupture at the same time. Satya Nadella, Microsoft's chief executive, testified that Microsoft was preparing to hire Altman and Brockman and other allies if OpenAI did not reinstate them during the 2023 crisis. Nadella's testimony also left Musk without a direct Microsoft warning: Musk did not raise concerns to him that Microsoft's investment violated special terms or commitments. Board authority collapsed quickly because it was already colliding with employee pressure, investor expectations, and partner dependence. If Sutskever was reacting to safety and trust failures, his vote can be argued as an attempt to enforce OpenAI's original restraints. Once workers and strategic backers resisted the move, the episode also exposed how little room the board had left to impose those restraints. Courts still have to separate two overlapping questions: whether the board had cause to move against Altman, and whether Microsoft's role changed OpenAI's mission enough to support Musk's broader claim. Directors now have to show whether the board acted from documented governance and safety concerns rather than from a power contest after Altman's allies rallied. Mission, Money, and Governance OpenAI's broader mission dispute is central to the case because the lawsuit turns on whether OpenAI abandoned its nonprofit mission as its for-profit arm expanded. Sutskever is trying to connect the board action to that institutional conflict by arguing that governance broke down after commercial incentives became too strong to contain. OpenAI's founding language gives that claim a benchmark. In 2017, Sutskever and Brockman warned about dictatorship risk from concentrated control over powerful AI systems. Early internal material from the same period framed the technology as something that should belong broadly to the world rather than to a financially motivated startup. "The goal of OpenAI is to make the future good and to avoid an AGI dictatorship. So it is a bad idea to create a structure where you could become a dictator." Ilya Sutskever in September 2017, former Chief Scientist at OpenAI Trial exhibits also include early OpenAI emails, photos, and corporate documents from before the lab had a formal name. Judges can compare that founding language with the company structure that later needed far larger capital commitments and operating scale. Commercial growth sharpened the contrast. Microsoft's more than $13 billion backing of OpenAI helped turn ChatGPT and the model stack into a business with heavy computing demands, strategic influence, and little tolerance for leadership paralysis. A small nonprofit lab could once afford internal disagreement over pace, oversight, and long-term risk. By contrast, a company supporting flagship AI products, premium cloud contracts, and enterprise customers faces far more pressure to keep leadership stable and product delivery predictable. Capital demands also changed the practical cost of dissent. A board confrontation that disrupted model development, cloud contracts, or commercial launches would no longer affect only a nonprofit research lab. It could hit a company already central to Microsoft's AI strategy and already carrying expectations from employees, customers, and investors. By 2023, OpenAI's research agenda needed large cloud capacity, customer confidence, and a partner ecosystem tied closely to Microsoft. Operating dependence now gives judges another test: whether the company's original structure could still function once OpenAI became too important, too expensive, and too interconnected for a small board to stop it abruptly. Fallout After Sutskever Left After Altman's return, the safety dispute did not end. Sutskever left OpenAI in May 2024, then launched Safe Superintelligence . OpenAI's safety-focused research group was disbanded days after he left in May 2024. Sutskever's departure carried the governance argument into 2024 instead of leaving it in 2023. His exit removed one of the board-crisis figures closely associated with long-term safety concerns, while the breakup of the superalignment effort weakened one of OpenAI's many visible internal structures for studying advanced-model risk. Safe Superintelligence gives the post-OpenAI split a live institutional marker. The new lab is built around the same superintelligence safety category that Sutskever linked to his concerns at OpenAI, while OpenAI continued scaling products inside a Microsoft-backed commercial structure. Later developments do not prove every courtroom claim Sutskever is making now. They do show that OpenAI's visible safety structure did not emerge stronger after the crisis. One path stayed inside OpenAI's commercial engine, while another moved into a separate lab built around the same long-term risk category. OpenAI and Safe Superintelligence now give that split a clearer institutional shape. OpenAI kept building inside a capital-intensive product business, while Sutskever moved into a lab meant to focus more narrowly on safe superintelligence. The divide does not resolve Musk's lawsuit, but it shows how personnel, research priorities, and governance assumptions continued to separate after Altman's return. The testimony ultimately frames the 2023 fight as more than executive drama. A founder who helped remove Altman still says the vote was meant to protect OpenAI, and the court now has to decide whether that account reflects a real mission breakdown or a failed internal revolt.

title: Googlebooks 💻, Starship v3🚀, Android's overhaul📱
teaser: Google is overhauling Android with Gemini, turning the phone into a multi-step task executor and rolling out vital anti-scam call defenses.
summary: Google is significantly revamping the Android ecosystem through Gemini Intelligence, moving the platform from a simple assistant to a powerful, multi-step task automation layer. Gemini, now powering features like Googlebooks (new AI-driven laptops), can execute complex workflows across apps and Chrome, making the phone act more like a system worker. Simultaneously, Google is strengthening platform security with Anti-scam call features and Android 17 upgrades, which introduce official-build verification and stricter app limits to enhance user safety. Beyond software, SpaceX is advancing with Starship Version 3, while Google maintains its interest in massive orbital data center projects with SpaceX.
author: TLDR
content: Google's Android-powered laptops are called Googlebooks, and they're coming this year (4 minute read) Googlebooks are designed from the ground up with Gemini intelligence. Wiggling the cursor on a Googlebook activates a full-screen Gemini experience. The AI can view screen content to make contextual suggestions, and it can pull in data from multiple apps. Googlebook devices will run Android and have access to the Play Store. Most manufacturers that make Chromebooks will also offer Googlebooks when they launch. Android is getting a big AI overhaul in 2026 (8 minute read) Google is expected to make several AI-related announcements at its I/O conference next week. App automation will be a major element of Android going forward. Gemini will power several new convenience features, including a custom widget feature. Almost everything new will arrive via Play Services, app updates, or on specific devices through partnerships rather than as a part of Android 17, which is slated to launch in June. Science & Futuristic Technology Once again, SpaceX has set a new record for the tallest rocket ever built (4 minute read) Starship Version 3, taller and more powerful than previous iterations, comes with numerous upgrades, including higher thrust, more efficient Raptor engines, a new reusable lattice-like structure at the top of the booster for hot staging, and three modified grid fins to help bring the first stage back to Earth for recovery and reuse. This version should be capable of in-orbit refueling. At a height of 408 feet, the rocket's upcoming flight (date yet to be determined) will mark the first liftoff from a new launch pad at Starbase. SpaceX and Google Are in Talks to Launch Data Centers in Orbit (5 minute read) Google is in talks with SpaceX and other rocket-launch companies for a rocket launch deal. Last year, Google announced Project Suncatcher, a moonshot initiative aimed at launching orbital data centers. Many industry leaders see orbit computing as a solution to the limitations of Earthbound data centers. SpaceX is also looking to launch orbital data centers. The speculative technology was the center of SpaceX's pitch to investors ahead of its planned IPO. Programming, Design & Data Science Redis and the Cost of Ambition (14 minute read) Projects developed as personal challenges and learning exercises are wonderful. However, without a solid use case, the maintainer will likely lose interest in the project and eventually abandon it. There's nothing wrong with the ambition to solve problems. Just don't lose sight of what made you successful in the first place. Why senior developers fail to communicate their expertise (7 minute read) Good senior developers aim to lower complexity. Adding to a system is risking more complexity, which creates instability. The rest of the company is focused on reducing uncertainty. Senior developers fail to communicate their expertise as they express their problems in terms of complexity management when they should be expressing their solutions in terms of uncertainty reduction. Apple Plans Customizable Camera for Pros, Siri Design Changes in iOS 27 (4 minute read) Apple plans to upgrade its Camera app to make it fully customizable. Users will be able to choose which features appear and where they're placed. The next major iPhone update will include other design changes, including system-wide changes such as new animations and redesigned tab bars. The update, which will include a revamped Siri, will be unveiled on June 8 at WWDC. Amazon employees are "tokenmaxxing" due to pressure to use AI tools (3 minute read) Amazon's MeshClaw product allows employees to create AI agents that connect to workplace software and carry out tasks on their behalf. It can initiate code deployments, triage emails, and interact with apps such as Slack. Some employees are using the software to complete unnecessary tasks to increase their consumption of tokens as the company is tracking their usage on internal leaderboards. Many employees have raised concerns about the security risks of AI tools that can act on users' behalf. What Is Code? (17 minute read) The future of coding is building better conceptual models, vocabularies, and foundations on top of which both humans and LLMs can work.

title: Kenya Delays $1B Microsoft-G42 Data Center Over Power Constraints
teaser: From Kenya to corporate policy: The rollout of $1B AI data centers is stalling globally due to insufficient local power grids and government approvals.
summary: Large-scale AI infrastructure projects are facing significant roadblocks, transforming complex clean-energy promises into urgent local logistical challenges. In Kenya, a proposed $1 billion Microsoft-G42 data center is stalled due to insufficient grid capacity—President William Ruto noted the power draw would destabilize the country's supply—and unresolved government approvals. Separately, Microsoft's commitment to 'hourly clean-power matching' for its AI buildouts is proving difficult to maintain. As AI demand surges, the company faces conflicts over real-time clean electricity supply, rates, and water usage. These global issues show that even highly ambitious tech infrastructure cannot proceed without stable local power grids, regulatory approval, and sustainable financial backing.
author: Markus Kasanmascheff
content: TL;DR Project Stall: Kenya is still trying to revive the Microsoft-G42 data-center plan, but power and approval constraints keep it stalled. Power Math: The proposed facility would draw roughly a third of installed capacity while Treasury clearance and guarantee terms remain unresolved. Regional Stakes: The delay leaves East Africa without a flagship Microsoft-G42 cloud build as rival infrastructure projects and regional demand keep moving. By May 10, Kenyan officials were still saying the stalled Microsoft-G42 data-center project may revive, but any restart depends on solving a basic constraint before construction can begin: the country's grid cannot easily absorb the facility's projected electricity demand. Officials have not treated the proposal as dead, and they still describe the talks as active. Kenya is keeping a $1 billion cloud and AI project in limbo even though expected demand equaled roughly a third of Kenya's installed power supply and Treasury approval also failed to arrive. Officials are now deciding whether the country can support the load, finance the commitment, and still make the site practical for customers and contractors. Kenya's president William Ruto summed up the power problem in unusually blunt terms. "To switch on that one data centre, we would need to shut off power for half the country. That's when I knew there was a problem." William Ruto, President of Kenya (via Business Insider Africa ) Kenya's electricity system is not dealing with a marginal increase in demand. Installed capacity stands at about 3,000 megawatts, so officials would have to balance one large industrial load against homes, businesses, and other public needs. Construction had not started, which means the plan is still stuck before any physical buildout can prove demand, secure customers, or lock in a realistic delivery timetable. Why the Project Hit a Wall Power was the clearest obstacle, but it was not the only one. Kenya's technology ministry prepared a concept note and submitted it to the National Treasury for funding review. Treasury approval did not follow, so the project lost the formal backing it needed just as electricity constraints were becoming harder to dismiss. A project proposal that failed to secure approval could not easily move into procurement, site preparation, or utility planning, even if the partners kept negotiating. Commercial terms created a second constraint. Officials also ran into a dispute over payment guarantees for committed computing capacity. Kenya was weighing grid capacity and fiscal exposure together, not one after the other. Negotiations could continue without Treasury support and commercially acceptable guarantees, but execution could not. Any guarantee would also have to fit a project whose customers, grid upgrades, operating costs, and construction schedule were still unsettled. A guarantee signed too early could leave the public sector exposed before the facility had dependable electricity, while a guarantee delayed too long could leave the partners without enough certainty to commit capital and equipment. Scale kept those pressures connected. The original plan called for an initial phase of around 100 MW, with scope to expand later. Developers expected the facility to sit near an Olkaria geothermal site northwest of Nairobi, while geothermal already supplies about 40% of Kenya's energy mix. One very large data center would still need dependable electricity every hour it runs, even with that renewable base. A 100 MW first phase would be large enough to shape grid planning before any later expansion, so backup capacity, transmission planning, land preparation, customer commitments, and construction timing all had to line up with the power model before the site could become a buildable plan. Official Response and Remaining Negotiations Kenyan officials are still trying to keep the plan alive. Philip Thigo, Special Tech Envoy Ambassador for the Kenyan government, said the government remains fully committed to the initiative despite electricity concerns. John Tanui, Principal Secretary in Kenya's ICT ministry, said talks still cover project structuring and power supply arrangements . His description keeps the proposal open. It also underlines what is still missing: a supply model that can carry the load, obligations the government is willing to accept, and an approval path that would let work restart without creating wider fiscal risk. Officials also continue to argue that the project had not been canceled. Contractors, prospective cloud customers, investors, and government planners still need a credible start date before treating the site as near-term infrastructure. An East Africa Azure region and a large local data-center build would shape latency, data-residency choices, procurement planning, electricity allocation, and the credibility of later digital-infrastructure pitches. For businesses, the distinction between active talks and a buildable project affects where they plan workloads, how they budget cloud migrations, and whether they can count on local capacity. Until the talks produce executable terms, those benefits remain potential rather than capacity companies can actually use. For officials, keeping the file open preserves negotiating room, but it also keeps pressure on ministries to show how power supply, Treasury clearance, and commercial obligations would work in practice. Timeline, Context, and Partnership Stakes Current delays look more serious because the project had already been slipping for months. In May 2024, the proposal was announced during Ruto's Washington visit, and that push was tied to the Microsoft and G42 partnership and to wider regional cloud ambitions. Microsoft and G42's package included plans for a geothermal-powered data center in Olkaria and an East Africa Azure cloud region. Kenya was not just courting another server facility. Officials were trying to anchor part of a larger cloud footprint in East Africa, where local capacity could shorten network paths, support data-location preferences, and give public-sector buyers a regional option for cloud and AI workloads. A local region would also let the partners sell the project as infrastructure for government services and enterprise AI use rather than only as another commercial hosting site. For Microsoft and G42, that regional promise depended on converting a diplomatic launch into a working site. The companies needed a location with power, permissions, customer demand, and a public-sector framework that could support long-running capacity commitments. Delays were already visible by the August 2025 meetings, when Kenyan officials and company executives had concluded that the original completion target would be missed. Washington had also given the alliance more visibility than a routine commercial expansion would usually receive. U.S. lawmakers' partnership scrutiny had already raised questions around the Microsoft-G42 relationship before Kenya's electricity bottleneck came into view. Kenyan officials also assembled the package with input from US and UAE governments as part of a push against China's Digital Silk Road presence in Africa. G42 drew scrutiny from US officials over its China ties before Kenya's local power problem became the main obstacle, adding another sensitivity around the partnership. A data-center project tied to governments, chip scrutiny, and AI infrastructure cannot rely only on branding once the host grid becomes the bottleneck. Microsoft and G42 need Kenya to demonstrate executable public commitments, while Kenya needs the partners to keep confidence in a project whose original delivery schedule already moved out of reach. The strategic frame can attract attention and capital, but it also raises the cost of a visible delay. A revival would need to reassure both sides at once: Kenya would need proof that the facility can operate without crowding out other users, and the partners would need confidence that approvals and guarantees will not slip again. East Africa Market and Competitor Environment Regional demand has kept moving while this project remains unresolved. Nxtra is building a 44 megawatt facility in Tatu City , which offers East Africa a smaller but tangible benchmark while AWS and Google Cloud keep competing for enterprise and public-sector workloads across Africa. Kenya's difficulty is not only about one delayed site. Power, approvals, and financing will shape whether the country can host the scale of build hyperscale providers and their partners expect when they commit serious capital. The Tatu City comparison also shows that smaller facilities can keep advancing while a much larger AI-oriented proposal remains exposed to national power planning. Power concerns became central enough that another industry account described the project as shelved . Ruto has used the episode to argue for 10,000 megawatts by 2030 , backed by broader investment plans meant to expand national generation. For this project, credible power expansion, Treasury clearance, and aligned construction approvals remain the checkpoints that would let contractors, customers, and investors treat the site as a live build.

title: Building a safe, effective sandbox to enable Codex on Windows
teaser: Codex can now run sophisticated coding tasks across your whole setup—from your local laptop to your phone—enabling seamless work even when you're away from your desk.
summary: OpenAI is significantly enhancing the safety and accessibility of its coding agent, Codex. On Windows, Codex's sandbox was redesigned to ensure maximum usability without sacrificing security. The new architecture uses synthetic SIDs and write-restricted tokens—rather than system tools like AppContainer—to allow the agent to function like a developer while strictly limiting file and network actions. Simultaneously, Codex's mobile app introduces a major usability upgrade, allowing users to stay in the loop from their phone. This enables users to review outputs, approve commands, and manage long-running coding tasks across multiple devices (including local laptops and managed remote environments) via a secure relay layer, fundamentally changing how developers collaborate with AI agents.
content: When I joined the Codex engineering team in September 2025, Codex for Windows didn't have a sandbox implementation meaning that Windows users were forced to choose between two subpar options when using OpenAI's coding agents: Approving nearly every command (even reads) that a coding agent wanted to run, which is inefficient and pesky. A major benefit of using Codex is that you don't have to do all the tedious work yourself. Enabling Full Access mode: letting Codex run all commands without approval or restrictions, which removes friction at the expense of oversight. Codex ⁠ , our coding agent, runs on developer laptops-whether that's through the CLI, the IDE extension, or the desktop app. It manages a conversation between a human at a keyboard and a model running in the cloud to handle inference. Codex runs with the permissions of a real user by default, meaning it can do everything the user can do. This is powerful and potentially dangerous. The coding model may tell the harness to run commands locally, from running tests to reading or editing a file to creating a Git branch, so Codex's default mode attempts to find the right balance between effectiveness and safety. This default mode allows Codex to read files almost anywhere and write files within your workspace (i.e., the directory where you're running Codex), with no internet access unless you specify you want it. To achieve this automatic constraint of writing files and accessing the network within safe bounds, Codex needs a sandbox environment that actually enforces these constraints. A sandbox is a constrained execution environment. When a developer uses Codex, their computer's operating system launches a command with reduced permissions, and those constraints propagate down the process tree. Every Codex command is sandboxed from the start, and every descendant process stays inside the same boundary. Codex needs isolation features enforced by the computer's operating system to implement an effective sandbox. Some operating systems provide utilities that do this well (e.g., Seatbelt on MacOs, seccomp or bubblewrap on Linux); however, Windows doesn't currently provide this type of capability out of the box. To make Codex just as safe and delightful to use on Windows as it already is everywhere else, we needed to implement our own sandbox. Windows offers some tools and primitives for isolation. While none of them quite met our requirements, we looked at a number of potential solutions-namely, AppContainer, Windows Sandbox, and Mandatory Integrity Control labeling. What: AppContainer is the native Windows sandbox, a capability-based isolation model built for apps that know, up front, exactly what they need to access. Why : Appealing because it offers a real OS boundary instead of best-effort restrictions. Why not : Codex is not one tightly scoped app. It drives open-ended developer workflows: shells, Git, Python, package managers, build tools, and whatever other binaries the agent decides it needs. In practice, that made AppContainer the wrong shape for the problem. It was strong isolation, but for a much narrower class of workloads than "let an agent operate like a developer." What: Windows Sandbox is Microsoft's disposable lightweight VM. You get a fresh Windows desktop with a strong isolation boundary, and whatever you do inside it disappears when the session ends. Why : Interesting for obvious reasons-far more compatible with arbitrary software than AppContainer, and from a security perspective it's a much stronger box. Why not : Codex needs to act directly on the user's actual checkout, tools, and environment, not inside a separate throwaway desktop that would need setup and host/guest bridging. It also had a fundamental product problem: Windows Sandbox isn't even available on Windows Home SKUs. Mandatory Integrity Control (MIC) integrity labeling What : Windows has a concept called "integrity levels," such as low, medium, and high, that determine how much the system trusts objects and processes. The basic rule is that a lower-integrity process cannot write to an object with a higher integrity level, even if the normal ACL would otherwise allow it. For example, a low-integrity process is treated as less trusted, so Windows blocks it from writing to normal medium-integrity objects, unless those objects are explicitly relabeled to allow it. Why : MIC looked elegant on paper-run Codex at low integrity, relabel the writable roots as low integrity, and let Windows enforce no-writes everywhere else. That would've given us a non-admin path with a real OS mechanism behind it. Why not : Like ACLs, integrity labels modify the real host filesystem, and in this case the semantic change is especially broad. Marking a workspace as low integrity does not just mean "Codex can write here." It means low-integrity processes in general can write there. On a real developer machine, that turns the user's actual checkout into a low-integrity sink for the host, which is much riskier than granting carefully targeted ACLs to one sandbox design. Even if medium-integrity developer tools continue to work, the underlying trust model of the workspace has changed in a way that's hard to contain and harder to justify. Having evaluated all of the options as non-starters, we started designing our own solution to bring a good Codex experience to Windows users. Our first working prototype used a combination of Windows concepts and tools to implement the isolation we needed. From the beginning, one goal was to make this work without requiring elevation , meaning that Codex would not need to prompt the user for administrator privileges just to set up or run the sandbox. That meant figuring out how to put reasonable limits on two things: file writes and network access. If we didn't limit file writes at all, we'd have a safety issue. If we limited file writes too much, the sandbox would hurt user productivity, needing to ask for constant approval. To solve this problem, we relied on two important Windows building blocks: SIDs and write-restricted tokens. A SID, or security identifier, is the identity Windows ties to permissions . Each user has a SID, groups have SIDs, and even a single login session gets its own SID. For example, a current logged-in session might have a SID like S-1-5-5-X-Y . The SID assigned to the local administrators group might be S-1-5-32-544 . Windows also lets you create synthetic SIDs that don't correspond to a real user but can still appear in ACLs (access control lists), which define who can read/write/execute specific files or directories. That makes SIDs a useful primitive for our sandbox: we can create SIDs exclusively for the Codex sandbox to use, without interfering with anything else on the machine. Process tokens are security objects in Windows that define identity and privileges for a running process. They determine what actions a process can perform. A write-restricted token is a particular type of process token that makes Windows perform an additional access check on write operations. In order for a write to succeed, two checks must pass: The normal user identity (the token "owner") must be allowed to do it At least one SID in the token's restricted SID list must also be granted access In practice, these checks let us use ACLs to define exactly where the sandbox could modify the filesystem, which offered the granularity we needed around write operations. With SIDs and write-restricted tokens, our unelevated sandbox worked like this: The sandbox setup created a synthetic SID called sandbox-write . The sandbox-write SID was granted write, execute, and delete access to The current working directory Any additional writable_roots configured in config.toml . The sandbox setup explicitly denied that same SID write access to "read-only within writable" locations such as: <cwd>/.git <cwd>/.codex <cwd>/.agents Codex launched commands under a write-restricted token whose restricted SID list includes Everyone , the current logged in session SID, and the sandbox-write synthetic SID. This flow effectively solved limiting file writes and seemed promising. Now we needed a solution for limiting the sandbox's network access. Limiting network access is an important part of the sandbox; without it, malicious code could exfiltrate data from the machine up to the internet. Because we wanted to avoid an elevation requirement, we had limited options to strongly block network traffic. The tools we wanted to use, like Windows Firewall, generally could not be installed without admin permissions. Without Windows Firewall as an option, we limited what we could control. We tried to make the child environment fail-closed for the kinds of networked tools developers actually use, so that Git commands, package installers, etc., would fail in the sandbox and the user would have to approve any internet-facing operations. The idea was to poison the obvious escape hatches: send proxy-aware traffic to a dead endpoint, make Git's HTTP(S) transport do the same, and make Git over SSH fail immediately. On top of that, we prepended a small denybin directory to PATH and reordered PATHEXT so stub SSH and SCP scripts would resolve before the real binaries. For example, here are some of the specific environment overrides we used to limit network access: HTTPS_PROXY=http://127.0.0.1:9 ALL_PROXY=http://127.0.0.1:9 GIT_HTTPS_PROXY=http://127.0.0.1:9 NO_PROXY=localhost,127.0.0.1,::1 GIT_SSH_COMMAND=cmd /c exit 1 That caught a lot of normal tool-driven traffic, but it was still only advisory. A process could ignore the environment, bypass PATH, or just open sockets directly-too risky. As with any interesting software implementation, the first prototype had some pros and cons. While it got the job done with only a few standard Windows capabilities, allowed for very explicit and granular filesystem writes, and ran unelevated-cutting the need for users to accept excessive elevation prompts or be admins on their local machine-it had some real drawbacks, some of which disqualified it from becoming our final design: Speed of setup: Applying workspace ACLs can be expensive depending on the topology of the workspace directory. Footprint: We applied real ACLs to the developer's system, although the footprint is not particularly invasive because all the applied ACLs pertain to a custom-created synthetic SID that is used only by the sandbox. Difficult-to-change semantics: The reliance on ACLs for file-based restrictions means it's expensive and complex to change sandbox semantics. Whereas on macOS, we can dynamically change how we generate the .sbpl file used to configure Seatbelt, the Windows sandbox could require a slow and intense operation to adjust ACLs. Network protection is weak. As mentioned before, it was "advisory," would definitely be circumvented by some programs that implemented their own networking stack, and wasn't designed to hold up to adversarial code. The first three issues are inherent to a custom sandbox implementation that's flexible enough for agentic flows. The network suppression story was different, though. In addition to a malicious agent being able to easily circumvent the environment-based network suppression, plenty of good-intentioned code/binaries would also circumvent it simply if they didn't honor the environment proxy variables, or if they implemented their own socket-based network code. We felt that this aspect was enough to consider investing in a better sandbox mode. To gain better network suppression, we wanted to use Windows Firewall, which allows us to block outbound network traffic for users or programs. Unfortunately, we couldn't effectively create a functional firewall rule that applied only to the commands spawned by the Codex harness for a few reasons: Windows doesn't allow matching a firewall rule to the non-principal identity of a restricted token. This means we couldn't apply a firewall rule to "any token that includes our synthetic SID in its restricted SID list." While we could create a firewall rule that matches a specific binary, that only allows us to limit networking for codex.exe itself. It wouldn't apply to the processes that the agent spawns on behalf of the user, like Git or Python processes. Other firewall match dimensions were the wrong shape, too. User-scoped rules still matched the real Windows user in the unelevated design, not just the restricted child. Program-path rules were too coarse: they could block codex.exe or python.exe generally, but not this one sandboxed invocation of python.exe . Port- or address-based rules were also the wrong policy entirely. For instance, we didn't want to block port 443; we wanted to block arbitrary outbound access for this specific restricted process tree. To apply a firewall rule specifically to our sandboxed commands, we needed to run them as a separate principal, not as the "real" user. This approach led us down a new path, one in which we relaxed our "no elevation" constraint. The next iteration of the sandbox, which is our current implementation, requires elevated admin permissions at setup time. I therefore refer to it as "the elevated sandbox." At the boundary where Codex spawns a command on the system, the elevated sandbox looks like the unelevated one. It still runs child processes under a restricted token-similarly a write_restricted token with the same restricted SID list of [Everyone, Logon, Synthetic ] -however, the principal of this token is no longer the actual Windows user but one of two local users created by Codex itself: CodexSandboxOffline (the one targeted by firewall rules) CodexSandboxOnline (the one not targeted by firewall rules) This seemingly small detail actually has big implications for the sandbox, who can use it, and the complexity of its setup and runtime execution. It's visually similar to the unelevated prototype, with the introduction of firewall rules and a dedicated Windows user, which actually runs the commands. (However, the introduction of these new concepts, means that there is more setup work to do before the sandbox can start running and protecting commands.) The unelevated sandbox design had a simple setup step, but it was relatively small: Create a synthetic SID if needed Apply ACLs for the sandbox-write synthetic SID The elevated sandbox, however, has more to do. Create a synthetic SID, if not already created Create the online and offline sandbox users, if not already created Store the newly-created users' credentials locally and encrypt using the Windows Data Protection API (DPAPI) in a place where the sandbox users cannot actually read Create firewall rules that block all outbound network access for the CodexSandboxOffline user or, if they already exist, validate they're correct There's an additional wrinkle in the setup stage. Codex's sandbox is expected to have read access equivalent to the actual Windows user. In the unelevated sandbox, where the restricted token's principal SID was the Windows user, this was achieved. However, that doesn't come for free when the principal becomes a new CodexSandbox user. Many relevant directories on Windows will grant read/execute permissions to "Authenticated Users". One notable example is the user's profile directory. By default, Windows users cannot read the profile directories of other Windows users, so even simple file reads in many scenarios would fail. To address this, we added another layer to the sandbox setup process-one for granting read ACLs to the sandbox users where such ACLs might not already exist. For example, to some commonly used Windows directories: C:\Users\<real-user> C:\Windows\ C:\Program Files\ C:\Program Files (x86)\ C:\ProgramData\ Because this list of directories is best-effort and installing ACLs on each one can be quite expensive, we run this logic asynchronously so the sandbox setup step, which is blocking to users, doesn't have to wait for them to complete. We encapsulated the setup logic in its own binary partly to cross the UAC boundary only when needed. But the deeper reason was architectural: sandbox setup has a fundamentally different job from codex.exe . Keeping the sandbox setup logic in a dedicated binary let codex.exe stay a normal, unelevated harness; kept the Windows-only setup machinery from bloating codex.exe on other platforms; decoupled longer-running setup work from the lifetime of the main process; and gave us one place to handle the different setup paths the sandbox needed. Because of how Windows user and token login boundaries work, we couldn't continue to create a restricted token and spawn a process under it the way we could with the unelevated sandbox. To actually spawn commands as a different Windows user, our first idea was the following flow: codex.exe runs as the real Windows user. Then, in a sequence, Codex: Calls LogonUserW(...) for the sandbox user. Calls CreateRestrictedToken(...) on that sandbox-user token. Using that restricted sandbox-user token, calls CreateProcessAsUserW(...) to launch the final child. In practice, that desired flow didn't work because of a privilege wall at CreateProcessAsUserW(...) . This means codex.exe could create a restricted token for the sandbox user, but it couldn't reliably launch a child with that token from the real-user side of the boundary. We needed a process that was already running as the sandbox user-this would let the restriction step and final spawn happen on the sandbox-user side of the boundary instead of the real-user side. That requirement led to codex-command-runner.exe , a new binary whose only job is to mint a restricted token and spawn the requested command. Instead of asking codex.exe to do the entire flow itself (real user → sandbox user → restricted token → child process), we split the flow in two: codex.exe calls CreateProcessWithLogonW(...) to launch codex-command-runner.exe as the sandbox user, without using a restricted token yet. Inside the runner, OpenProcessToken(GetCurrentProcess(), ...) opens the runner's own token, which already belongs to the sandbox user. The runner calls GetTokenInformation(...) to extract the sandbox logon SID, then CreateRestrictedToken(...) to build the final restricted token. Still inside the runner, it calls CreateProcessAsUserW(...) with that restricted token to launch the real child. Albert Einstein said, "Everything should be made as simple as possible, but no simpler." In that spirit, our design adequately solved each problem. The final architecture has the four layers we have previously covered: codex.exe itself codex-windows-sandbox-setup.exe for handling all elevated setup related work codex-command-runner.exe for running restricted token commands The child process When I first approached this project, I did not have a strong sense of where it would wind up. My approach was to start by instrumenting the sandboxing capability in the boundary between Codex and the operating system. This approach closely matches how Codex's sandbox is implemented on MacOs and Linux. As I learned more about the specific tools that Windows provides, and through dozens of decisions balancing security and ease of use, the system grew to its current form-multiple binaries, custom users, firewall rules, an elevated setup step, asynchronous processes, and more. It's not a particularly simple system, but each piece of complexity was added out of necessity, to build a sandbox that is both safe and, as much as possible, not in the user's way. Working to deliver a good user experience for Codex users on Windows, our goal was to make something safe that didn't compromise on usefulness-the whole point of using Codex is to have agents be able to do work without your constant attention. One of the biggest lessons from this project was that Windows did not hand us one primitive that cleanly maps to "safe autonomous coding agent." We composed several tools and concepts to build something coherent. Some early ideas were dead ends. The final design was a hybrid of earlier prototypes that each solved part of the problem. The other lesson was that security for a coding agent is a different beast than more classic application security. Codex has to work for real developer workflows. The engineering work was about balancing compatibility with agentic workloads against real enforcement. That tension shaped tradeoffs in the final design. Curious to see the Codex sandbox in action? Try it out ⁠ .

title: Clarity Act Latest Draft 📜, The Anatomy of Credit 💳, Alpenglow live for testing🧪
teaser: The convergence of AI and finance is accelerating, moving the industry toward regulated infrastructure layers and sub-cent payments for agentic commerce.
summary: The crypto and AI sectors are rapidly maturing, shifting focus from speculative exchange trading to fundamental infrastructure and institutional integration. The proposed Clarity Act in the US aims to regulate stablecoins, DeFi, and crypto assets, providing necessary legal guardrails. This trend is accelerated by 'agentic commerce,' where protocols like x402 enable sub-fraction-of-a-cent payments for AI compute, highlighting a move toward machine-to-machine economies. However, DeFi's vast lending market is hampered by a lack of core credit infrastructure—like tranching—despite Real-World Assets (RWAs) surpassing $28B. Infrastructure build-out continues with dedicated platforms like BaiBai (PropAMM) on Base, and institutional positioning favoring entities like Coinbase, which provides a critical, integrated stack for this next wave of regulated, high-volume commerce.
author: TLDR Crypto
content: Senate Unveils Crypto Market Structure Bill Ahead of Vote (5 minute read) The US Senate Banking Committee released the latest draft of the Clarity Act, outlining rules for stablecoin yields, DeFi protections, and broader crypto market structure as it heads toward a key committee vote. While the bill preserves legal safeguards for DeFi developers, unresolved conflicts around ethics provisions and stablecoin interest limits highlight the remaining hurdles before potential passage. Dolphin Network Targets Idle GPU Inference Market (4 minute read) Dolphin Network routes AI inference jobs across idle consumer GPUs in a peer-to-pool model, directing 100% of protocol revenue toward open-market $POD buybacks to offset emissions. The pricing structure captures a $0.20/M token margin on Qwen 3.6 35B inference at $0.70/M versus OpenRouter's $1.00, positioning Dolphin 30% below the cheapest centralized provider while paying nodes $0.50/M. Token design draws from veCRV boosts, xSUSHI/yCRV auto-compounding, stAAVE cooldowns, and vlCVX bribe markets, with a 20% liquid-claim fee routing to the xPOD vault and a bond-duration multiplier reaching 2x beyond six months. A forthcoming paper titled "Encrypted Live-Weight Proofs for Decentralized Inference" addresses model-correctness verification across all hardware types, extending coverage beyond TEE-only NVIDIA cards. BaiBai Launches First PropAMM Platform on Base (5 minute read) BaiBai is the first PropAMM (Proprietary Automated Market Maker) platform on Base. It enables professional market makers to update pricing, depth, and inventory onchain tens to hundreds of times per second, a strategy that already dominates Solana DEX volume but has been blocked on EVM chains by expensive storage writes and toxic order flow outpacing stale quote updates. BaiBai is built on Spire Labs' Pylon, a high-performance EVM appchain providing dedicated maker blockspace with cheap price-curve updates, instant block times, and full synchronous composability to the Base settlement chain without requiring users to bridge assets. Pylon's custom sequencing rules place maker updates at the top of each block while imposing a speed bump on toxic flow, directly addressing the front-running problem that has prevented PropAMMs from functioning on EVM. BaiBai also operates as a smart liquidity router, filling a portion of orders against its own quotes and routing the remainder to external liquidity, targeting tighter spreads than centralized exchanges on Base for market makers, aggregators, solvers, and sophisticated traders. The Anatomy of Credit: DeFi Lending Without a Credit Market (6 minute read) DeFi's $10B+ lending economy, anchored by Aave, Morpho, and Compound, operates without the core credit infrastructure traditional markets depend on: tranching, native credit ratings, and CDS instruments, which force all lenders into identical risk/yield profiles regardless of risk appetite. Real-world credit assets have reached scale onchain, with RWAs crossing $28B, ERC-4626 vaults holding $16B+, BlackRock's BUIDL at billions in AUM, and instruments such as Apollo's $ACRED and Figure's HELOCs (cutting ~120bps in funding costs) demonstrating institutional demand for tokenized credit. Serotonin's State of Onchain Credit maps 160+ teams, yet only four (Cork, Strata, Royco, and Pendle) address tranching and risk management, the mechanism that allows Goldman and JPM to slice pools into senior, mezzanine, and equity tranches for differentiated capital allocation. Cork Protocol positions itself as the onchain tranching layer, and without senior/mezzanine/equity pricing, DeFi's single-number yields cannot attract the institutional capital flows needed to build a credit market beneath the lending economy. Venice ($VVV): The Bubble's Mirror (10 minute read) Venice is the structural inverse of closed AI lab valuations: OpenAI and Anthropic require the model layer to stay premium, a premise now being arbitraged away as Chinese open-source models grew from 1.2% to 30% of global usage in 2025. Venice carries zero training cost, TEE-attested cryptographic privacy (vs. OpenAI's policy-based model, which was implicated in a Mixpanel/DNS exploit leaking customer data), and a buyback-and-burn mechanic that has eliminated 42% of genesis supply. Growing agentic payment rails concentrate demand on KYC-free inference providers, and Venice's metrics reflect the thesis: 50B tokens/day, VVV up from $2 to $18 over three months, DIEM discount compressed from 57% to 32%. Repricing Coinbase For The Agent Economy (6 minute read) Markets price Coinbase as a crypto exchange when it should be valued as financial infrastructure for agentic commerce, as card rails at $0.03-0.04 per transaction are uneconomical for sub-cent AI API calls that stablecoins settle in seconds for fractions of a cent. Coinbase holds the only vertically integrated stack for this use case, pairing USDC, Base, and CDP/AgentKit/x402 developer infra, while Stripe remains card-rail anchored, Visa and Mastercard's unit economics break below one cent, and Circle's Arc product is not yet live. The thesis gained enterprise validation when x402 and Coinbase wallet infrastructure were integrated into Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Payments, and since October 2025, x402 has processed 178.7M agentic payments totaling $42.4M across 5,000+ merchants, with 82.1% settling on Base and 99.8% in USDC. The bull case applies a 20% stablecoin capture rate to McKinsey's $7.5T agentic commerce projection for 2031, yielding $1.5T in annual volume and roughly $4.25B in annual Coinbase revenue from USDC float, developer infra, facilitator economics, and Base settlement fees. Starknet Introduces Private Bitcoin Wrapper strkBTC (4 minute read) strkBTC is a shielded Bitcoin wrapper that uses zero-knowledge proofs to enable private balances and confidential transfers while remaining composable across DeFi. The design adds compliance features like viewing keys for auditability, positioning it as "private onchain cash" amid rising security risks tied to transparent blockchain data. Bhutan Sells Another 100 BTC (3 minute read) Bhutan's government transferred 100.44 BTC worth about $8.2 million, adding to more than $230 million in Bitcoin outflows this year and leaving the country with roughly 3,119 BTC valued at about $252 million.

title: Enterprise AI race 🏃, AI P&L shifts📉, becoming AI native 🤖
teaser: Traditional SaaS margins of 70% may plummet to 17% due to AI's personalized demands, forcing a total business model overhaul.
summary:
The rise of AI fundamentally reshapes the economics of software, challenging the traditional SaaS model. While older SaaS enjoyed high gross margins (around 70%), AI-native software may see margins capped significantly lower, potentially at 17% due to the personalized nature of AI calls, which removes cost-saving efficiencies like multi-tenancy. To adapt, businesses must become 'AI-Native' by moving implicit knowledge (like pricing logic or refund policies) into explicit, machine-readable workflows.

In terms of tooling, GitHub Copilot is changing its billing model, introducing a usage-based system starting June 1st. While Pro and Pro+ plans maintain their stated price points, usage is now allocated through 'flex allotments' and 'base credits,' signaling a shift where heavy, agent-style workloads are increasingly metered. Furthermore, Anthropic recently passed OpenAI in business adoption, while Recursive Superintelligence continues raising capital ($650M+) for self-improving AI, demonstrating the accelerating pace of industry development.
author: TLDR Founders
content: How AI changes software P&L (12 minute read) Saas used to mean 70% gross margins. AI-native software might cap at 17%. Every AI call is personalized, so caching and multi-tenancy don't reduce your costs. Reasoning models burn 10-100x more tokens than the ones they replaced, so cost per task barely moves even as per-token prices drop. The math: 1 million users at $120 ARPU still leaves you at 17% gross, 11% net. That's consumer goods territory, not Salesforce. Four ways out: 1/10-cost clones (no moat), niche/lifestyle businesses (now viable since build costs collapsed), luxury software (Raya, Bloomberg Terminal), or vertical integration into atoms or services. If your deck still assumes 80% margins because that's what SaaS does, rewrite it this week. How to become "AI-Native" (8 minute read) AI-native is an organizational label, not a tech one. It is estimated that only roughly 1,000 companies above $5M ARR have actually rebuilt themselves so agents can operate inside the core workflows rather than at the edges. Most companies aren't legible to machines because pricing logic lives in "Final_v7_NEW" spreadsheets, refund policy hides in a Notion doc nobody trusts, and the sales process is "talk to Sarah," so the AI-native shift requires making implicit knowledge explicit: documented decision rules, agent-readable SOPs, clean customer objects, permissions, audit trails, and evaluation loops. I closed 70m in ARR in 2 years. Here's exactly how (15 minute read) Nicolas Brillante added over $70 million in ARR at Slash without a playbook. This post provides a bit of background on Brillante to explain who he is and how he achieved this feat. He started reselling digital items when he was 12 years old to buy a new computer. That early success kept him going, and he ended up managing multiple businesses. How winners pivot (6 minute read) A pivot is any change that rewires your unit economics, not a 180-degree rebuild. Before you change anything, map your entire conversion funnel in a FigJam, every marketing touchpoint, landing page, demo, lifecycle, trial, and retentive user, with the conversion percentage written between each step. The worst drop-off tells you which lever to pivot. Then test the pivot MVP-style with five different funnels for the five ICP groups you think will be stickiest, each with its own creative, landing pages, and email sequences. The worst mistake is broadcasting the pivot to the world before you have retentive paying beta testers. GitHub Copilot individual plans: Introducing flex allotments in Pro and Pro+, and a new Max plan (3 minute read) GitHub Copilot Pro and Pro+ plans now include more total usage at the same price through a new flex allotment. Paid plans now include base credits - once users go beyond that base, a flex allotment is applied automatically, and users can purchase more usage to keep going if they run out of tokens. Code completions and next edit suggestions remain unlimited on paid plans and don't consume credits. A new Max plan has been introduced for sustained, high-volume Copilot work. Automate progressive rollouts with Vercel Flags (1 minute read) Vercel Flags is a new tool for rolling out features to a growing percentage of users on a schedule. It supports progressive rollouts that gradually shift the traffic percentage to the new variant. Each stage has a target percentage and a duration. Exposing changes in stages allows developers to catch regressions on a small slice of users before they hit everyone. Public Stealth Leaves Opportunity on the Table. Working in Secret is Even Worse (6 minute read) Founders often harm their prospects by staying too secretive about their efforts. Having no public trace of their startup work, such as a domain or LinkedIn update, can cause them to miss out on critical connections and opportunities. Basic visibility, like a personal domain or relevant LinkedIn job listing, helps signal commitment and legitimacy to potential investors and partners. 10x is a lot (3 minute read) There's a gap between claiming 10x and what 10x actually looks like in the wild. Real 10x is the gap where the old way stops making sense, email vs fax, Stripe vs wire transfers, not "23% faster but rounded up." Run the test before you write "10x" in your hero copy and ask whether your buyer would say the word unprompted on a call. If they wouldn't, you're padding.
